Progressive Encephalomyelitis with Rigidity and
Myoclonus with an Aggressive Presentation
Mimicking Septic Shock: A Pediatric Case Report
and Literature Review
Samuel C.S. Ho 1 K. Y. Leung 1 Grace S.F. Ng 1 W. L. Yiu 1 Eric K.C. Yau 1 N. C. Fong 1
1 Department of Pediatrics and Adolescent Medicine, Princess
Margaret Hospital, Kwai Chung, Hong Kong
J Pediatr Neurol 2023;21:462 –466.
Address for correspondence Samuel C.S. Ho, MBBS, MRCPCH,
Department of Pediatrics and Adolescent Medicine, Princess Margaret
Hospital, 2-10 Princess Margaret Hospital Road, Kwai Chung, Hong
Kong (e-mail: samuelho11@gmail.com).
Introduction
Progressive encephalomyelitis with rigidity and myoclonus
(PERM) is a relapsing –remitting neurological disorder that
falls within the stiff person syndrome (SPS)-spectrum dis-
orders. In addition to axial and limb rigidity typical of SPS,
PERM is associated with encephalopathy, brainstem, and
autonomic dysfunction.
1,2
We present a case of PERM with a unique initial presen-
tation mimicking fulminant septic shock. We also performed
a PubMed search with the keywords “progressive encepha-
lomyelitis with rigidity and myoclonus, ”“ PERM,” and “stiff
person syndrome. ” We reviewed all pediatric PERM cases
that were published before January 1, 2023.
Case Report
A 16-year-old previously healthy Chinese girl presented to
emergency department with acute impaired consciousness,

syndrome
► glutamic acid
decarboxylase
► dysautonomia
Abstract Progressive encephalomyelitis with rigidity and myoclonus (PERM) is a relapsing–remitting
neurological disorder that falls within the stiff person syndrome –spectrum disorders. We
report a 16-year-old girl with PERM associated with an anti-glutamic acid decarboxylase
(GAD) antibody. She had an aggressive initial presentation mimicking fulminant septic
shock, followed by truncal and lower limb rigidity, stimulus-sensitive spasm, cognitive
impairment, brainstem signs (hyperekplexia, nystagmus), and dysautonomia (urinary
retention, constipation, facial ﬂushing, blood pressure ﬂuctuation). Cerebrospinal ﬂuid,
electroencephalography, and magnetic resonance imaging of the brain and spine showed
features suggestive autoimmune encephalitis and myelitis. The serum anti-GAD antibody
was positive, and the diagnosis of PERM was made. She had ﬂuctuating clinical response
despite intravenous immunoglobulin, steroids, plasmapheresis, and symptomatic medi-
cations. Eventually, in the fourth month since admission, she showed gradual and persistent
clinical improvement after introducing rituximab. She was discharged after 6 months of
hospitalization, and no relapse was observed in the ﬁrst 3 years of follow-up.
PERM is a rare and underrecognized condition in children. Contrary to previous reports,
our case describes an aggressive and life- threatening presentation for PERM. Vague
symptoms and the lack of gold diagnostic te sts hinder a timely diagnosis. Our study
also highlights the need for developing stand ardized diagnostic criteria and consensus
in managing PERM.

urinary incontinence, bilateral lower limb stiffness, and
1-week history of low-grade fever. She had no prior drug
intake. Upon admission, she was unresponsive with respira-
tory distress, hyperthermia (41.8°C), hypotension
(53/21 mm Hg), and tachycardia (180/min). She was intu-
bated, given inotropic support, empirical antibiotics, anti-
epileptics, and midazolam infusion and sent to pediatric
intensive care unit. Her limb stiffness subsided after the
administration of midazolam.
Initial investigation showed raised creatine kinase
(108,510 IU/L; normal: <144 IU/L) and troponin I (88,874
ng/L; normal: <21 ng/L), deranged renal function, metabolic
acidosis, rhabdomyolysis, and disseminated intravascular
coagulation (
►Supplementary Table S1 , available in online
version). Echocardiogram showed poor cardiac contractility,
and the computed tomography brain was normal. Based on
the above ﬁndings, the initial impression was myocarditis
and encephalitis with septic shock and systemic in ﬂamma-
tion. She became more alert and showed clinical improve-
ment after hemodialysis and intravenous immunoglobulin
(IVIg) given on the ﬁrst day of admission.
On the ﬁfth day of admission, however, her stiffness
recurred after extubation and weaning of sedation. Upon
examination, she had board-like rigidity over the abdomen,
paraspinal muscles, and bilateral lower limbs with ﬁxed
extension. She was observed to have hyperekplexia, episodic
painful muscle spasms, and myoclonus spontaneously or
triggered by tactile stimuli and emotional stress. She also
showed cognitive impairment with disorientation, rambling
speech, disinhibition, and retrograde amnesia.
Extensive microbiological, metabolic, and toxicological
tests were unremarkable. Serological workup was otherwise
unremarkable, besides the high antinuclear antibody (1:160)
and positive anti-Ro antibody. Cerebrospinal ﬂuid (CSF)
showed mild pleocytosis (10/mm
3) with normal protein,
negative oligoclonal band, and a negative autoimmune panel
including anti-N-methyl-d-aspartate receptor, anti-contac -
tin-associated protein-like 2, anti-leucine-rich glioma inac -
tivated 1, anti- α-amino-3-hydroxy-5-methyl-4-isoxazole
propionic acid receptor, anti-dipeptidyl-peptidase-like pro-
tein-6, and anti-gamma-aminobutyric acid (anti-GABA) B1/
B2. Electroencephalogram (EEG) revealed generalized delta
brush waves and magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) of the
brain showed subtle hyperintensity in bilateral medial tem-
poral lobes on T2 and ﬂuid-attenuated inversion recovery
sequence (
►Fig. 1A ), both suggestive of autoimmune en-
cephalitis. Electromyogram (EMG) was challenging to inter-
pret as she was uncooperative. Given the new clinical
ﬁndings, the diagnosis aligned with SPS with autoimmune
encephalitis. She received a second course of IVIg, methyl-
prednisolone, and symptomatic medications (diazepam,
baclofen, gabapentin) for her rigidity and painful spasm.
Serum anti-glutamic acid decarboxylase (GAD) antibody
was sent to an immunology laboratory outside our hospital
for testing. However, testing for anti-glycine receptor (GlyR)
antibody and CSF anti-GAD antibody were unavailable due to
limitations in our locality. In addition, positron emission
computed tomography was performed to screen for associ-
ated tumors, which showed unremarkable results except an
incidental ﬁnding of thyroiditis.
Over the next few weeks, she developed transient nystag-
mus and autonomic dysfunction, including urinary reten-

tion, constipation, facial ﬂushing, and blood pressure
ﬂuctuation. Voiding cystourethrogram showed features of
neurogenic bladder, and MRI spine suggested myelitis with
mildly swollen spinal cord and bilateral T2 hyperintense
signal extending from the 10th to 11th thoracic vertebral
level to conus medullaris (
►Fig. 1B ). Serum anti-GAD anti-
body returned positive (170 IU/mL; cutoff: <10 IU/mL).
Given the additional brainstem signs and dysautonomia, a
diagnosis of PERM was made, supported by the above
radiological and serological evidence.
She had ﬂuctuating clinical response despite a repeated
third course of IVIg and plasmapheresis in subsequent months.
Eventually, in the fourth month since admission, she showed
gradual and persistent clinical improvement after introducing
rituximab. Clinically, both limb stiffness and spasm subsided,
and her cognitive function returned to baseline. Repeated EEG,

EMG, MRI, and anti-GAD level (8 IU/mL) also returned normal.
She was discharged after 6 months of hospitalization. She
complained of residual stiffness over paraspinal muscles with
marked thoracolumbar scoliosis and hyperlordosis (
►Fig. 1C )
and was treated surgically with posterior spinal fusion and
bone graft a year after discharge. No relapse was observed in
the ﬁrst 3 years of follow-up.
Discussion
The differential diagnoses of acute or subacute onset of
stiffness and spasm in children are broad ( ►Table 1 ). SPS
should be considered when stimulus-sensitive stiffness and
spasms involve the torso and lower extremities. When there
are other cognitive, brainstem, and autonomic dysfunction,
PERM should be highly suspected. Diagnostic workup
includes lumbar puncture, MRI, EEG, EMG, tumor screening,
and a full antibody panel from serum and CSF
2,3 (►Table 1 ).
In 2022, Newsome and Johnson proposed diagnostic
criteria for all SPS-spectrum disorders, including classic,
partial, SPS-plus, pure cerebellar ataxia, and PERM
1
(►Supplementary Table S2 , available in online version).
Compared with other variants of SPS, PERM has a wide array
of clinical manifestations. This is exempli ﬁed by our patient
who developed muscle stiffness, spasm, encephalopathy
(disorientation, disinhibition, retrograde amnesia), dysauto-
nomia (urinary retention, constipation, facial ﬂushing, blood
pressure ﬂuctuation), and brainstem signs (hyperekplexia,
nystagmus). CSF pleocytosis, EEG ﬁnding of generalized delta
brush waves, and abnormal MRI results characteristic of
PERM further supported the diagnosis.
Anti-GAD antibody plays a considerable role in the clinical
manifestation of PERM, as seen in our case. The inhibitory
effect on GAD blocks the synthesis of GABA at the brainstem
and spinal cord,
4 enhancing motor excitability with muscle
stiffness and spasm. 2 The inhibition of GAD at the hippo-
campus and prefrontal lobes, on the other hand, contributes
to her cognitive impairment, disinhibition, and amnesia.
2,4
PERM is a rare and underrecognized condition in children.
In 2021, Chang et al reviewed 81 PERM cases across all ages,
and only ﬁve were pediatric cases.
5 To our knowledge, only
eight pediatric PERM cases, including ours, have been
reported thus far. Their clinical manifestations, investigation
ﬁndings, and management are summarized in
►Table 2 .
Most were presented at 14 to 18 years old with heteroge-
neous clinical features. Most patients presented with stiff-
ness ( n ¼ 8), spasm ( n ¼ 8), and brainstem signs ( n ¼ 7),
whereas cognitive impairment ( n ¼ 3) and dysautonomia
(n ¼ 2) were less commonly reported.
In contrast to other pediatric cases, our patient had an
aggressive presentation mimicking fulminant septic shock.
Similar presentations were reported in some adult PERM cases
with sudden death.
2 While the exact mechanism remains
unclear, autonomic dysfunction crises, spasmodic storms, met-
abolic acidosis, and respiratory failure have been proposed.2
This case highlights the diagnostic challenges for PERM in
children. Similar to previous cases, clinical manifestation at
an early stage is often nonspeci ﬁc and misleading. 1 Her
initial presentation was highly suggestive of an infective
cause, and the distinctive features of PERM only became
apparent in later weeks. Therefore, appropriate evaluation
was delayed, including anti-GAD antibodies not included in
the initial workup. While EMG can show co-contraction of

agonist and antagonist muscles in SPS,
1 it was deemed
unhelpful in our case as she was uncooperative. Due to our
locality, a full antibody panel is not immediately available.
Besides, the interpretation of anti-GAD antibodies may be
affected by the previous use of IVIg, which was considered
life-saving and should not be withheld. These are all
obstacles to allowing a timely diagnosis of PERM.
According to our literature review, anti-GAD antibody
(n ¼ 4; 50%) is more prevalent than anti-GlyR antibody
(n ¼ 2; 25%) among pediatric patients, contrary to the ﬁnd-
ings in adult patients.
1,2,5 No signiﬁcant difference in clinical
outcome is noted among children with different antibody
proﬁles, whereas adults with an anti-GlyR antibody are
reported to have better treatment outcomes.
4 However, it
is essential to note that most pediatric PERM cases currently
lack evaluation of a complete antibody panel. With the
discrepancy between children and adults, our literature
review highlights the importance of future studies on

understanding different antibodies ’ diagnostic and prognos-
tic roles in children. Developing standardized diagnostic
criteria and a clinical scoring system will also be helpful.
Currently, there has yet to be an established consensus on
PERM management. Similar to adult cases,
1–3,5 most pediat-
ric cases received a combination of symptomatic medica-
tions (benzodiazepines, baclofen) and immunotherapy.
Similar to Newsome and Johnson ’s proposal, 1 we adopted
the escalation approach of immunotherapy: ﬁrst line with
IVIg, steroid, or plasmapheresis, the second line with ritux-
imab or mycophenolate mofetil, third line with cyclophos-
phamide, and ﬁnally fourth line with stem cell therapy. Early
initiation of immunotherapy is advocated, best within
2 months of disease onset.
5 However, as demonstrated in
our patient, treatment response tends to ﬂuctuate during the
acute disease phase before consistent improvement later.
Residual sequelae and relapses are common; hence, follow-
up is essential for long-term monitoring of symptoms.
Contrary to previous reports, our case describes an ag-
gressive and life-threatening presentation of PERM in chil-
dren. Vague symptoms and the lack of gold diagnostic tests
hinder a timely diagnosis. Our study also highlights the need
for developing a standardized diagnostic criterion and con-
sensus in managing PERM.

None declared.

EMG, MRI, and anti-GAD level (8 IU/mL) also returned normal.
She was discharged after 6 months of hospitalization. She
complained of residual stiffness over paraspinal muscles with
marked thoracolumbar scoliosis and hyperlordosis (
►Fig. 1C )
and was treated surgically with posterior spinal fusion and
bone graft a year after discharge. No relapse was observed in
the ﬁrst 3 years of follow-up.

segments.text:
Compared with other variants of SPS, PERM has a wide array
of clinical manifestations. This is exempli ﬁed by our patient
who developed muscle stiffness, spasm, encephalopathy
(disorientation, disinhibition, retrograde amnesia), dysauto-
nomia (urinary retention, constipation, facial ﬂushing, blood
pressure ﬂuctuation), and brainstem signs (hyperekplexia,
nystagmus). CSF pleocytosis, EEG ﬁnding of generalized delta
brush waves, and abnormal MRI results characteristic of
PERM further supported the diagnosis.
Anti-GAD antibody plays a considerable role in the clinical
manifestation of PERM, as seen in our case. The inhibitory
effect on GAD blocks the synthesis of GABA at the brainstem
and spinal cord,
4 enhancing motor excitability with muscle
stiffness and spasm. 2 The inhibition of GAD at the hippo-
campus and prefrontal lobes, on the other hand, contributes
to her cognitive impairment, disinhibition, and amnesia.
2,4
PERM is a rare and underrecognized condition in children.

segments.text:
In contrast to other pediatric cases, our patient had an
aggressive presentation mimicking fulminant septic shock.
Similar presentations were reported in some adult PERM cases
with sudden death.
2 While the exact mechanism remains
unclear, autonomic dysfunction crises, spasmodic storms, met-
abolic acidosis, and respiratory failure have been proposed.2
This case highlights the diagnostic challenges for PERM in
children. Similar to previous cases, clinical manifestation at
an early stage is often nonspeci ﬁc and misleading. 1 Her
initial presentation was highly suggestive of an infective
cause, and the distinctive features of PERM only became
apparent in later weeks. Therefore, appropriate evaluation
was delayed, including anti-GAD antibodies not included in
the initial workup. While EMG can show co-contraction of

1 it was deemed
unhelpful in our case as she was uncooperative. Due to our
locality, a full antibody panel is not immediately available.
Besides, the interpretation of anti-GAD antibodies may be
affected by the previous use of IVIg, which was considered
life-saving and should not be withheld. These are all
obstacles to allowing a timely diagnosis of PERM.
